Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 74
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Widowed
  occupation: Combat Pilot
  trauma_type: Physical abuse by romantic partner
  pcl5: 56

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Tactile (Touch): Physical touch, Offender Cues: Seeing the offender, Olfactory (Alcohol): Alcohol smell
  Maladaptive Strategies: Suppress Anger: never allow myself to feel or express anger, Avoid Perpetrator Cues: Anything that reminds me of the person who harmed me, Avoid Intimacy: Being emotionally close or intimate with others
  Threat: Sleep Vigilance: I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert, Hypervigilance: Being superalert or watchful or on guard, Physical Reactivity: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience

Vignette:
Frank is a 74-year-old retired combat pilot, a widower of twelve years, who came to the clinic at the urging of his daughter. He had been living alone in the same suburban house for three decades, and for the last several years, his world had been steadily shrinking. The event that had reshaped everything for him was not a dogfight or a crash landing, but something that had happened in his own home, decades ago, with a woman he had loved. His second wife, Carol, had been a heavy drinker. On a night he could still feel in his bones, she had come home reeking of whiskey, and an argument had turned violent. She had struck him repeatedly across the face and chest, screaming accusations he could no longer remember. He had not fought back. He had been a man trained to kill from the sky, and he had frozen, pinned against the kitchen counter by a woman half his size. The shame of that moment, of his own paralysis, had become a permanent fixture in his mind.

In the months and years that followed, Frank had not spoken of it. He had left Carol shortly after, but the damage was already done. He found that he could no longer tolerate the sensation of being touched unexpectedly. A pat on the back from a friend at the VFW made him flinch, his shoulders knotting up. A hand on his arm from his daughter would send a jolt through him, and he would pull away before he could stop himself. He told himself it was just because he was getting older, more set in his ways. But he knew, deep down, that the feeling of another person’s hand on his skin had become linked to that moment of helplessness. He had also begun to avoid any reminder of Carol. He threw away her photographs, cleared her belongings from the house, and stopped driving past the bar where she used to drink. He even stopped buying certain brands of whiskey, because the smell alone—that sharp, sweet odor of alcohol—would make his stomach turn and his heart race. He would find himself scanning a room at a family gathering, checking for wine bottles, and would leave early if anyone opened one.

The most profound change, however, was in his relationships. Frank had always been a reserved man, but after the assault, he became a fortress. He never allowed himself to feel or express anger. When his daughter would press him about his health or his isolation, he would feel a hot surge of something in his chest, but he would swallow it down, his face going blank. He was certain that if he ever let that feeling out, he would lose control completely, become violent, and prove that he was the monster Carol had accused him of being. He had also stopped seeking out any form of emotional closeness. He turned down invitations to dinner, declined offers from a neighbor to watch football, and let his few friendships wither. It was safer this way, he reasoned. If no one got close, no one could hurt him again. The consequence was a profound loneliness that he felt most acutely at night, when the house was silent.

Sleep had become a battleground. Frank had difficulty falling asleep because he felt he needed to stay alert. He would lie in bed, rigid, listening to every creak and groan of the house, his mind running through escape routes. He was constantly on guard, even in his own home. During the day, he was hypervigilant. On his weekly trip to the grocery store, he would position himself with his back to a wall, watching the aisles. If he saw a woman with a similar build to Carol, or caught the scent of alcohol on another shopper’s breath, his hands would start to shake and his heart would pound so hard he felt dizzy. These physical reactions were automatic, and they terrified him. He had come to believe that his body was no longer his own, that it was still back in that kitchen, waiting for the next blow.

What finally brought Frank to seek help was a panic attack at his granddaughter’s birthday party. His daughter had placed a hand on his shoulder to guide him to the cake, and the smell of a red wine stain on the carpet had hit him at the same moment. He had frozen, unable to speak, his vision tunneling. He had left without an explanation, driving home in a cold sweat. The next day, his daughter had called, her voice thick with worry, and he had agreed to see someone. He was terrified of what was happening to him, of the fortress he had built, but he was even more afraid of losing the only person who still tried to reach him. He hoped, though he could barely admit it to himself, that there might be a way to feel safe without being so utterly alone.
